newsitem.title: UK: Labour, unions look at ways to halt UK strike wave.
newsitem.headline: Labour, unions look at ways to halt UK strike wave.

text.p: A British trade union leader called on Sunday for a binding arbitration system as a way to end labour disputes, a controversial idea among the unions but one that may find favour with the Labour Party.
Britain has been hit by a wave of disputes this summer, and Ken Jackson, general secretary of the big AEEU engineers union, said more could be expected as the economy picked up.
The Labour Party looks set to win the next election, due by mid-1997, and Jackson told a news conference this could "usher in a new era of partnership between companies and employees."

"This gives us a great opportunity to put strikes behind us and have, in their place, a better way of settling disputes," he said, suggesting "small, fast-track Arbitration Appeal Units" whose decisions would be binding on unions and employers.
He made it clear this should be a voluntary system. Unions and employers would have to agree to arbitration, but would then be obliged to accept verdicts.
"We're not talking about about legislation to ban strikes or impose binding arbitration," he said.
Jackson said he had not discussed his idea with Labour Party officials.

Nor, it turned out, had he discussed it with his delegation to the Trades Union Congress conference, which begins here on Monday, and AEEU President Davey Hall apparently showed his disagreement by boycotting the news conference.
The plan could find favour with Labour employment spokesman David Blunkett, who is to address a fringe meeting on Tuesday.
However, according to a report in the Sunday Times, he is examining an even more radical system, including the use of compulsory binding arbitration to resolve disputes.
The newspaper said this would be seen by the unions as "a backdoor way of banning strikes."
Labour leader Tony Blair upset the unions during the summer when he said a dispute on the London underground system ought to be put to arbitration, against the wishes of the union involved.
TUC general secretary John Monks told a separate news conference he welcomed ways of minimising disruption from strikes, but he was against imposed arbitration.
"Arbitration works best when all parties to a dispute agree that it's the best way of resolving that dispute," he said.
Bill Morris, general secretary of the Transport and General Workers Union, agreed, and made the point that it was often employers who stood out against arbitration procedures.
"No employer that I know is prepared to hand over critical areas (of management policy) to a third party," he said.
